The (Mississippi) Delta blues was a rootsy sparse style with passionate vocals accompanied by slide guitar.
In addition to Robert Johnson, influential performers of this style included his predecessors [[Charley Patton]] and [[Son House]].
was in 1923 the first to record the [[slide guitar]] style, in which a guitar is fretted with a knife blade or the sawed-off neck of a bottle
Several record companies, such as the [[American Record Corporation]], [[Okeh Records]], and [[Paramount Records]], began to record African-American music.
The notion of blues as a separate genre arose during the [[Great Migration (African American)|Black migration]] from the countryside to urban areas in the 1920s
[[Howlin' Wolf]], Muddy Waters, [[Willie Dixon]] and [[Jimmy Reed]] were all born in Mississippi and moved to Chicago during the Great Migration.
Chicago became a center for electric blues from 1948 on, when [[Muddy Waters]] recorded his first success, "I Can't Be Satisfied".
which, together with [[jazz]] and [[gospel music]], became a component of R&B.
